n: very short simple way psychiatry formulation

faq.a: It links the diagnosis to the patient’s story, guiding personalised treatment and communication.
faq.q: Why use a formulation instead of just a diagnosis?

faq.a: Yes, it should be updated as new information or response to treatment emerges.
Include each domain when relevant; some cases may be dominated by one factor.
faq.q: Do I need all three biopsychosocial domains?

exam: Explain the components of a biopsychosocial formulation for a patient with new‑onset psychosis.
List three red‑flag features that mandate urgent referral in a depressive presentation.
Describe how you would choose an antipsychotic for a patient with schizophrenia and a history of cardiac disease.
ai.subject: Psychiatry
ai.summary: A psychiatry formulation is a concise, structured narrative that links a patient's history, symptoms, and context to a working diagnosis and management plan. It helps clinicians think logically and communicate clearly.

b: Identify the primary psychiatric diagnosis
Note any comorbid medical or substance issues
sections.p: A formulation summarises why a patient is unwell, using a biopsychosocial lens, and links symptoms to recognised diagnostic criteria (e.g., DSM‑5, ICD‑10).

b: Mild, moderate, severe categories
Acute vs chronic phase
sections.p: Rate severity with standard scales (e.g., PHQ‑9 for depression, PANSS for psychosis) to guide intensity of treatment and monitor change.

b: Genetic predisposition or neurochemical imbalance
Recent stressors, trauma, loss
Social factors: isolation, poverty, stigma
sections.p: Consider biological, psychological and social contributors, prioritising the most plausible based on history and setting.

b: Mood, thought, perception, behaviour changes
Impairment in work, relationships, self‑care
sections.p: Describe core symptoms, their duration, and functional impact, linking each to the diagnostic criteria.
Use targeted tests to rule out medical mimics and support treatment decisions.

t.b: Is there anemia or infection that could mimic or worsen psychiatric symptoms? Low Hb may suggest iron deficiency depression; high WCC may point to infection.
Are thyroid abnormalities contributing to mood or anxiety? Elevated TSH supports hypothyroidism; low TSH suggests hyperthyroidism.
Is substance use influencing presentation? Positive cannabinoids or stimulants may explain psychosis or agitation.

b: Suicidal intent with plan
Psychotic agitation with risk to self/others
Rapid deterioration in cognition
sections.p: Identify features that require urgent intervention or signal worsening.

b: Antidepressants for moderate‑severe depression (increase serotonergic tone)
Antipsychotics for psychosis (dopamine blockade, avoid high EPS risk in elderly)
Psychotherapy (CBT, supportive) to address thoughts and coping
Lifestyle: sleep hygiene, regular activity, substance avoidance
sections.p: Treat underlying causes, then apply evidence‑based pharmacological and psychosocial interventions, explaining rationale.

b: Re‑assess severity scales every 2–4 weeks initially
Educate patient/family on early warning signs
Vaccination, infection screening in high‑risk settings
sections.p: Schedule regular reviews to monitor response, side‑effects and relapse risk; plan relapse‑prevention strategies.

b: Hypothyroidism vs depression
Cerebral malaria vs psychosis
Substance‑induced mood disorder vs primary mood disorder
sections.p: Conditions that can mimic psychiatric presentations.

Negative drug screen may miss recent use of short‑half‑life substances

Rapid loss of consciousness or new neurological signs
